questions.question: What does it mean for $f$ to be right-continuous at $x_0$?
options: For $x$ sufficiently close to $x_0$ with $x \lt x_0$, the values $f(x)$ are close to $0$.
The value $f(x_0)$ must be the largest value of $f$ near $x_0$.
The function must be defined on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
For $x$ sufficiently close to $x_0$ with $x \ge x_0$, the values $f(x)$ are close to $f(x_0)$.

questions.question: Let $f(x) = 2$ for $x \ge 0$ and $f(x) = 1$ for $x \lt 0$. Which statement is true at $x_0 = 0$?
options: $f$ is left-continuous at $0$.
$f$ is both left-continuous and right-continuous at $0$.
$f$ is neither left-continuous nor right-continuous at $0$.
$f$ is right-continuous at $0$.

questions.question: Let $f(x) = x+1$ for $x \le 0$ and let $f(0) = 1$. Which epsilon-delta condition directly matches left-continuity at $0$?
options: For every $\varepsilon \gt 0$ there is $\delta \gt 0$ such that $0 \lt x \lt \delta$ implies $|f(x)-1| \lt \varepsilon$.
For every $\varepsilon \gt 0$ there is $\delta \gt 0$ such that $|f(x)| \lt \varepsilon$ for all $x$.
For every $\varepsilon \gt 0$ there is $\delta \gt 0$ such that $-\delta \lt x \le 0$ implies $|f(x)-1| \lt \varepsilon$.
For every $\delta \gt 0$ there is $\varepsilon \gt 0$ such that $x \lt 0$ implies $|f(x)| \lt \delta$.

questions.question: At an integer $k$, which statement is true for the ceiling function $f(x)=\lceil x\rceil$?
options: $f$ is left-continuous at $k$
$f$ is right-continuous at $k$
$f$ is fully continuous at $k$
$f$ has no one-sided continuity at $k$

questions.question: Suppose $f$ is defined on $(x_0-r,x_0+r)$ for some $r>0$. Which condition is equivalent to continuity of $f$ at $x_0$?
options: The left-hand and right-hand limits at $x_0$ exist and are equal, with no condition on $f(x_0)$.
At least one of left-continuity and right-continuity at $x_0$ holds.
$f$ is continuous at every point of $(x_0-r,x_0)$ and at every point of $(x_0,x_0+r)$.
$f$ is both left-continuous and right-continuous at $x_0$.

questions.question: Let $f\colon[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f(0)=3$ and $f(x)=3+x$ for $x>0$. Is $f$ right-continuous at $0$?
options: No, because $f(x)$ is not constant for $x>0$.
Yes, because $f(x)=3+x\to3=f(0)$ as $x\to0^{+}$.
No, because $f$ is not defined for $x<0$.
Yes, because the value $f(0)=3$ is defined.

questions.question: Let $f\colon[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$. Which condition is equivalent to continuity of $f$ at the endpoint $0$?
options: $f$ is right-continuous at $0$.
$f$ is both left-continuous and right-continuous at $0$.
$f$ is left-continuous at $0$.
The right-hand limit $\lim_{x\to0^{+}}f(x)$ exists.

questions.question: Let $f\colon[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=x+1$ for $x>0$. Is $f$ right-continuous at $0$?
options: Yes, because the right-hand limit $\lim_{x\to0^{+}}f(x)$ exists.
No, because the right-hand values approach $1$, not $f(0)=0$.
Yes, because $f(0)<f(x)$ for every $x>0$.
No, because $f$ is not defined for $x<0$.

questions.question: Let $f\colon[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be given by $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=\sin\frac{1}{x}$ for $x>0$. Is $f$ right-continuous at $0$?
options: Yes: $f$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ and $f(0)=0$ is defined.
Yes: for $\varepsilon=2$ any $\delta>0$ works, as $|f(x)-f(0)|\leq1$.
No: the right-hand limit exists, but it differs from $f(0)=0$.
No: for $\varepsilon=\frac{1}{2}$, each $(0,\delta)$ has an $x$ with $f(x)=1$.
